lessons.title: Nanoparticles and surface area
lessons.summary: Find out what nanoparticles are, why their tiny size gives them a huge surface area to volume ratio, and how that leads to new uses and new risks.
objectives: I can compare the sizes of nanoparticles, fine particles and coarse particles using standard form.
I can calculate surface area to volume ratios and explain how they change as particles get smaller.
I can explain why nanoparticles have different properties from the same material in bulk.
I can describe uses of nanoparticles and evaluate the possible risks.

activities.title: How small is nano?
activities.content:
## Particle sizes

A **nanometre (nm)** is one billionth of a metre: $1\ nm = 1 \times 10^{-9}\ m$. A human hair is about 80 000 nm across, and a single atom is roughly 0.1 nm.

Scientists sort small particles by diameter:

| Type | Diameter | In standard form |
|---|---|---|
| Coarse particles (dust, PM10) | 2500 nm to 10 000 nm | $2.5 \times 10^{-6}$ m to $1 \times 10^{-5}$ m |
| Fine particles (PM2.5) | 100 nm to 2500 nm | $1 \times 10^{-7}$ m to $2.5 \times 10^{-6}$ m |
| **Nanoparticles** | **1 nm to 100 nm** | $1 \times 10^{-9}$ m to $1 \times 10^{-7}$ m |

A nanoparticle contains only a few hundred atoms. That is far bigger than a single atom or a small molecule, but far smaller than anything you can see, even with an ordinary microscope.

**Converting units:** to change nm to m, multiply by $10^{-9}$. So 50 nm = $50 \times 10^{-9}$ m = $5 \times 10^{-8}$ m. Be ready to write these numbers in standard form in the exam.

question.text: A particle has a diameter of 40 nm. Which category does it belong to?
question.hint: Nanoparticles are between 1 nm and 100 nm.
question.explanation: 40 nm is within the 1 nm to 100 nm range, so it is a nanoparticle. Fine particles start at 100 nm.

options.feedback: Fine particles are 100 nm to 2500 nm.
An atom is about 0.1 nm, 400 times smaller.

activities.title: Surface area to volume ratio
activities.content:
## The big idea

The most important thing about nanoparticles is their **surface area to volume ratio**.

Take a cube with sides of length $L$:
- surface area = $6L^2$ (six faces)
- volume = $L^3$
- ratio = $6L^2 \div L^3 = 6/L$

The ratio is $6/L$, so **as the side length gets 10 times smaller, the ratio gets 10 times bigger**.

| Side length | Surface area | Volume | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 cm | 600 cm² | 1000 cm³ | 0.6 |
| 1 cm | 6 cm² | 1 cm³ | 6 |
| 1 mm | 6 mm² | 1 mm³ | 6 (per mm) |

Why does this matter? Chemistry happens at **surfaces**. A nanoparticle has a huge proportion of its atoms on the outside, where they can react, catalyse or interact with light. A lump of the same material has almost all its atoms buried inside, doing nothing.

This is also why a powder burns faster than a block and why catalysts are used as fine powders or thin coatings.

activities.title: Worked example: calculating the ratio
activities.content:
**Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 2 nm, and compare it with a cube of side 20 nm.**

*2 nm cube:*
- surface area = 6 × 2² = 6 × 4 = **24 nm²**
- volume = 2³ = **8 nm³**
- ratio = 24 ÷ 8 = **3**

*20 nm cube:*
- surface area = 6 × 20² = 6 × 400 = **2400 nm²**
- volume = 20³ = **8000 nm³**
- ratio = 2400 ÷ 8000 = **0.3**

The side length went up 10 times and the ratio dropped to one tenth. Put the other way round: shrinking a particle 10 times multiplies its surface area to volume ratio by 10.

A quick check: the ratio for a cube is always $6/L$. For $L = 2$ that is 3, and for $L = 20$ it is 0.3. Use this shortcut to check your working.

question.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 5 nm. Give your answer as a decimal.
question.hint: Surface area = 6 × side², volume = side³. Then divide.
question.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 25 = 150 nm². Volume = 125 nm³. Ratio = 150 ÷ 125 = 1.2.

activities.title: Why nanoparticles behave differently
activities.content:
## New properties from old materials

Because so many of their atoms are at the surface, nanoparticles often have **different properties from the bulk material** even though they are chemically the same substance.

- **Catalysis.** Gold is famously unreactive as a metal, but gold nanoparticles are effective catalysts because the huge surface area gives reactions somewhere to happen.
- **Colour and light.** Bulk gold is yellow; gold nanoparticles in solution can appear red or purple. Titanium dioxide is a white pigment in paint, but as nanoparticles it is **transparent**, which is why it is used in sunscreens that block ultraviolet light without leaving a white smear.
- **Melting point and strength.** Nanoparticles can melt at lower temperatures than the bulk material, and mixing them into a plastic can make it stronger or more electrically conductive.

A valuable practical consequence: because the surface area is so large, **smaller quantities of a nanoparticle catalyst are needed** compared with the bulk material to get the same effect. That saves money and reduces waste.

question.text: True or false: nanoparticles of a substance can have different properties from the same substance in bulk form.
question.hint: Think about titanium dioxide in paint versus in sunscreen.
question.explanation: True. The very high surface area to volume ratio changes how nanoparticles interact with light and other substances, so their properties can differ from the bulk material.

activities.title: Uses of nanoparticles
activities.content:
## Where nanoparticles are used

| Use | Nanoparticle | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Sunscreens | titanium dioxide, zinc oxide | absorb and reflect UV but are transparent on skin |
| Medicine | silver, gold, lipid nanoparticles | silver is antibacterial; particles can carry drugs to specific cells |
| Cosmetics | various | deliver moisturiser deeper into skin; make products spread evenly |
| Catalysts | platinum, gold, palladium | enormous surface area means less metal is needed |
| Deodorants and wound dressings | silver | kill bacteria |
| Electronics | carbon-based, metal oxides | make tiny circuits and better batteries |

Notice the pattern: most uses come back to either **surface area** (catalysts, antibacterial action) or **size** (small enough to pass into cells or to be invisible on skin).

When an exam asks you to *explain* a use, name the property (surface area, transparency, antibacterial) and link it to what the product needs. "It is small" on its own is rarely enough for the mark.

question.text: Match each nanoparticle use to the property that makes it work.
question.hint: Sunscreen needs to be invisible; deodorant needs to stop bacteria; catalysts need lots of reacting surface.
question.explanation: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are transparent so sunscreen is not white; silver nanoparticles kill bacteria; catalyst nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio.

pairs.right: Transparent on the skin while blocking UV
Very high surface area to volume ratio

activities.title: Risks and unknowns
activities.content:
## Should we be cautious?

Nanoparticles are new enough that their **long-term effects are not fully known**, and the very features that make them useful also raise concerns.

- **Getting into the body.** Nanoparticles are small enough to be breathed in, absorbed through the skin or pass into cells. Once inside, they might build up in organs. What happens next is still being researched.
- **Toxicity.** Some nanoparticles that are harmless as bulk materials may be harmful at the nano scale because their high surface area makes them more reactive, and they may catalyse unwanted reactions in cells.
- **The environment.** Silver nanoparticles washed out of clothing or dressings can end up in rivers and might kill helpful microorganisms.
- **Lack of data.** Because products are relatively new, there are few long-term studies of people exposed to them for decades.

A balanced answer weighs benefits (effective sunscreen, less catalyst needed, targeted medicines) against risks (unknown toxicity, environmental harm) and often concludes that **more research and clear labelling** are needed so people can make informed choices.

activities.title: Worked example: evaluating a sunscreen
activities.content:
**A student says nano-sunscreens should be banned until they are proven safe. Evaluate this view.**

*For the sunscreen:* titanium dioxide nanoparticles block UV very effectively and are transparent, so people are more likely to wear the product, reducing skin cancer risk. Studies so far suggest the particles do not pass through healthy skin.

*Against:* nanoparticles might pass through damaged skin or be inhaled from sprays. Long-term effects on the body and on marine life (when washed off in the sea) are not fully known.

*Conclusion:* a complete ban would remove a product with clear benefits. A stronger position is to allow use with **labelling**, avoid spray forms that can be inhaled, and continue research into long-term effects.

The skill here is giving both sides and then a justified conclusion, not just listing facts.

question.text: Which of the following are reasonable concerns about the use of nanoparticles? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Concerns are about their small size and how new they are.
question.explanation: Nanoparticles may be absorbed into the body and their long-term effects are not fully understood. They are not radioactive, and they do not lose surface area (they gain it).

options.text: They may be absorbed into cells and their long-term effects are unknown
They could harm organisms if released into the environment

options.feedback: Being small does not make a particle radioactive.

options.text: They have a much smaller surface area than bulk materials
options.feedback: The opposite: they have a far larger surface area to volume ratio.

question.text:
Silver nanoparticles are added to some socks to stop them smelling.

(a) A silver nanoparticle has a diameter of 25 nm. Write this diameter in metres in standard form. (1 mark)

(b) Explain why silver nanoparticles are more effective at killing bacteria than the same mass of silver as a single lump. (2 marks)

(c) Suggest one possible disadvantage of using silver nanoparticles in socks. (2 marks)
question.hint: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m. For (b), think about where atoms are in a nanoparticle. For (c), think about washing.
question.explanation: (a) 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. (b) Nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio, so far more silver atoms are at the surface where they can contact and kill bacteria. (c) Nanoparticles may wash out into waste water and harm useful bacteria or aquatic life; long-term effects on people are not fully known.

markScheme.criterion: Nanoparticles have a much larger surface area to volume ratio
So more silver atoms are at the surface in contact with bacteria
Nanoparticles may be washed out / released into the environment
Could harm organisms / long-term effects unknown / could be absorbed by the body

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Nanoparticles** are 1–100 nm across ($1 \times 10^{-9}$ to $1 \times 10^{-7}$ m) and contain only a few hundred atoms.
- For a cube, surface area to volume ratio = $6/L$: **shrinking a particle 10 times multiplies the ratio by 10**.
- High surface area means nanoparticles have **different properties** from the bulk material and **less material is needed** for catalysts.
- Uses: sunscreens (transparent, block UV), medicine (drug delivery, antibacterial silver), cosmetics, catalysts, electronics.
- Risks: can enter cells, unknown long-term effects, possible environmental harm; more research needed.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the size range of nanoparticles?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nanoparticles are between 1 nm and 100 nm in diameter.

options.feedback: That is the fine particle range.

practiceQuestions.text: Convert 8 nm into metres. Give your answer as a number multiplied by 10⁻⁹ (just enter the number).
A cube has sides of 10 nm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Surface area = 600 nm², volume = 1000 nm³, ratio = 0.6.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: as a particle gets smaller, its surface area to volume ratio gets smaller too.
practiceQuestions.hint: Remember the 6/L rule for a cube.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Smaller particles have a larger surface area to volume ratio.

metadata.blanksText: Nanoparticles of titanium dioxide are used in sunscreens because they block ___ light but are ___ on the skin.

practiceQuestions.hint: The harmful part of sunlight; and a word meaning see-through.
practiceQuestions.explanation: They block ultraviolet (UV) light and are transparent, so they do not leave a white layer.

practiceQuestions.text: Arrange these from smallest to largest.
practiceQuestions.hint: An atom is about 0.1 nm; a hair is tens of thousands of nm.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Atom (0.1 nm) < nanoparticle (1–100 nm) < fine particle (100–2500 nm) < coarse particle (2500–10 000 nm).

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why a smaller mass of a nanoparticle catalyst is needed compared with the same catalyst in bulk form.
practiceQuestions.hint: Where do reactions happen on a catalyst?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reactions take place on the surface of a catalyst. Nanoparticles have a much larger surface area to volume ratio, so a small mass provides a large surface for the reaction.

markScheme.criterion: Nanoparticles have a larger surface area to volume ratio / more surface for the same mass
Reactions occur at the surface, so more catalyst atoms are available to react

practiceQuestions.text: A cube of side 1 nm is cut into cubes of side 0.1 nm. By what factor does the total surface area to volume ratio increase?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 6/1 = 6 and 6/0.1 = 60, so the ratio increases by a factor of 10.

options.feedback: Volume changes by 1000 and area by 100, but the ratio of the two changes by 10.

practiceQuestions.text:
Some face creams contain nanoparticles that are claimed to carry moisturiser deeper into the skin.

Evaluate whether people should use these creams. Include at least one advantage and one disadvantage, and give a justified conclusion.
practiceQuestions.hint: Advantage: what the nanoparticles let the cream do. Disadvantage: what we do not yet know. Conclusion: what should happen next.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Advantage: nanoparticles can pass deeper into the skin so the product may work better. Disadvantages: they may be absorbed into the body and their long-term effects are unknown; they could also enter the environment when washed off. Conclusion: people can use them but should be informed through labelling, and more research is needed before we can be sure they are safe.

markScheme.criterion: Advantage: nanoparticles penetrate deeper / product is more effective
Disadvantage: may be absorbed into the body / enter cells
Long-term effects are unknown / not enough research
Justified conclusion, e.g. use with labelling / more testing needed / benefits outweigh risks

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are uses of nanoparticles? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two are real uses; two are not.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Silver nanoparticles are used in antibacterial wound dressings and nanoparticles are used as catalysts. Nanoparticles are not used to make bulk steel girders or as a fuel.
